clue.text: Approach twice for censorious comment

blocks.note: to approach is to draw near, a simple synonym
the same word again, as 'twice' instructs

explanation.surface: Someone is told off for making a critical remark on two occasions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' simply asks you to write the synonym for 'Approach' a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: The doubled phrase is a mild spoken rebuke, uttered to express disapproval or tell someone they are being unreasonable.

clue.text: Ranks putting energy into throws

indicators.note: putting one thing into another places it inside, the first half of a split instruction
into marks the destination, so the preceding piece ends up inside the following one

blocks.note: to cast is to throw
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Troops in formation are put to work hurling things.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is split around its object: 'putting energy into throws' puts E inside CASTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Castes are hereditary social classes, so they are ranks or strata within a society's hierarchy.

clue.text: Insubstantial, somewhat irksome? Agreed

indicators.note: somewhat means only partly, so just a part of the following words is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone concedes that a flimsy argument is a bit annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and full stop between the two words are ignored; the letters are read straight through irksoME AGREed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something meagre is scanty or lacking in quantity or quality, so it has little real substance.

clue.text: Poet seeing tip of esker between mountain pass and elevation

indicators.note: the tip of something is its point or end, here its very first letter
to sit between two things is to be flanked by them, so one piece goes inside the others

blocks.note: a col is a pass or low point between mountain peaks
an esker is a long ridge of glacial gravel; its opening letter is kept
a ridge is a raised strip of land, an elevation

explanation.surface: A poet on a walking tour spots a glacial feature in the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's geological vocabulary is apt for a Lake District poet, but each word is working separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was the English Romantic writer of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner and Kubla Khan.

clue.text: Madman eagerly represented Biblical figure

indicators.note: to represent is to present again in another form, so the letters take a new shape

blocks.note: taken as written for their letters

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic lunatic plays a character from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented' reads like acting a part, but it is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the follower of Jesus in the Gospels who witnessed the crucifixion and first saw him risen.

clue.text: Custodian visibly pained twice in retreat

indicators.note: a retreat is a movement backwards, so the letters are read from the far end

blocks.note: skin that is red shows soreness
a second word for visibly pained: raw skin is sore and inflamed

explanation.surface: A guard, clearly hurt more than once, falls back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twice' is unusual: it asks for two different synonyms of the same phrase, as in the idiom 'red raw', before the whole pair is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A warder is a prison guard, someone who has people in custody and keeps watch over them.

clue.text: Take fish

blocks.note: first meaning: a noun, one's particular viewpoint or slant on something
second meaning: a verb, to try to catch with rod and line

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an instruction to catch something; in fact 'Take' is a noun, as in 'what's your take on it?'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a point of view on a matter and the activity of fishing with a hook and rod.

clue.text: Costly accessories suit

blocks.note: first meaning: expensive gems worn as jewellery
second meaning: one of the four sets in a pack of playing cards

explanation.walkthrough: 'suit' looks like clothing to go with the accessories, but it is the card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: The precious stones are prized jewellery, and the red suit marked with lozenges is one of four in cards.

clue.text: Scripture considered to have morally improved ...

blocks.note: RE is religious education, the school subject once called Scripture
to deem is to consider or judge

explanation.surface: Bible study is judged to have made someone a better person, a thought the ellipsis carries into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: RE, religious education, is the British school subject covering Scripture; the ellipsis links the surface to 10 down and plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To be redeemed is to be saved from sin or to have made up for past faults, becoming a better person.

clue.text: Plaster moulded for stationery item

indicators.note: something moulded is shaped into a new form, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written for its letters

explanation.surface: Plaster of Paris is shaped into a desk ornament.
explanation.walkthrough: Moulding is exactly what one does with plaster, which hides the fact that 'moulded' is the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A stapler is a desk tool for fastening sheets of paper together, one of the standard office supplies.

clue.text: No good tucking into antelope in part of kingdom

indicators.note: to tuck into is to get inside something, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: NG is the standard abbreviation for no good
an eland is a large African antelope

explanation.surface: A worthless animal eats its way into an antelope somewhere in a realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucking into' tempts you to picture eating, but it means going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: England is one of the four nations making up the United Kingdom, along with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

clue.text: ... lay readers opt out: they anticipate what's coming

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so these letters are not in their proper arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written for their letters

explanation.surface: Continuing from 8 down: church lay readers choose to withdraw, being people who foresee the future.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opt out' reads as a phrase, but 'opt' belongs to the letters and 'out' alone is the signal. A lay reader is a non-ordained person licensed to lead parts of church services.
explanation.definitionFit: Early adopters are the first customers to take up a new technology, ahead of the trend before others catch on.

clue.text: Mistake, ignoring onset of extreme fear

indicators.note: to ignore the onset is to leave out the beginning, so the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: terror is extreme fear

explanation.surface: Someone blunders by failing to notice the first signs of panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'onset of extreme' tempts you to drop the E of extreme, but the onset belongs to the whole phrase's synonym, TERROR.
explanation.definitionFit: An error is a blunder or slip, the plainest synonym for getting something wrong.

clue.text: Spooner's rough method in which 'i's are dotted twice

definitions.text: method in which 'i's are dotted twice

indicators.note: Dr Spooner famously swapped the first sounds of words, so the opening sounds are exchanged

blocks.note: coarse means rough and a mode is a method; swap their opening sounds

explanation.surface: A crude way of writing in which every i gets two dots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dotting the i's' suggests fussy precision, but here it is literal: in the signalling system the letter I is sent as two dots.
explanation.definitionFit: In this telegraph alphabet each letter is a pattern of short and long signals, and I is two short ones.

clue.text: Stroke family pet with ping-pong bat

blocks.note: a doggy is a childish word for a dog, the classic family pet
a table-tennis bat is also called a paddle

explanation.surface: Someone pats the household animal with a table-tennis bat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stroke' looks like a verb about petting the animal; it is a noun, a swimming stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the simple swimming style where arms and legs paddle underwater, as a dog swims.

clue.text: Reported dodgy act: no deal

indicators.note: something dodgy is unreliable or crooked, so the letters are not straight

blocks.note: taken as written for their letters, ignoring the colon

explanation.surface: A news item: a shady manoeuvre, and no agreement reached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reported' can look like a past tense verb, but here it is an adjective, as in reported rather than verified evidence.
explanation.definitionFit: Anecdotal evidence rests on hearsay and personal accounts passed on by others rather than on systematic study.

clue.text: Still cheats, first to last

indicators.note: moving what is first to the last place rotates the word by one position

blocks.note: to swindle is to cheat

explanation.surface: A fraudster carries on cheating, going from one victim to the next.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' reads as 'even now', but it is the definition, the adjective for calm air.
explanation.definitionFit: Still weather has no breeze at all, so a calm, motionless day is one without any wind.

clue.text: Like a damning review describing low-budget film?

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase, as the answer is an adjective

blocks.note: first meaning: a critic's rating of no stars out of five
second meaning: a cheap film cannot afford famous actors

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are about film criticism, but 'star' is used in two senses: a rating symbol and a celebrity actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Reviews award stars as a grade, and big-name actors are called stars, so a film can lack either kind.

clue.text: Taking joint, he's addled, not entirely able to control matters ...

indicators.note: taking means lifting a part out of something larger, here from inside the words
not entirely means only partly, so the final letter of the run is not used

blocks.note: the letters run from inside the first word through to just before the end of the last

explanation.surface: A man who has smoked a joint is befuddled and not wholly in charge, the ellipsis carrying on into 20 across.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the comma and apostrophe: joINT HE'S ADDLEd holds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from riding: a rider in the saddle is in charge, so someone in that position holds command.

clue.text: Emulate a bird: leave in haste

blocks.note: first meaning: to copy a bird is to flap one's wings, which a bird does with rapid strokes
second meaning: slang for go away quickly

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is whimsical: a bird beats its wings to fly off, and flying off is exactly leaving in a hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang imperative tells someone to clear off quickly, and a bird escapes by rapidly flapping its wings.

clue.text: Sealed the deal; shut down the business

blocks.note: first meaning: completed a sale or agreement
second meaning: ceased trading permanently

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are business deals, which makes them look like one story; they are two senses of one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To close a sale is to finalise an agreement, and to close a firm is to stop trading altogether.

clue.text: ... gossip: fellow taking methamphetamine with little price to pay

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: dirt is scandalous gossip
a chap is a man or fellow
E is slang for ecstasy, a drug derived from methamphetamine

explanation.surface: Scandal story, continued from 17 across: a man on crystal meth pays hardly anything.
explanation.walkthrough: Ecstasy is methylenedioxymethamphetamine, so the setter lets its crossword letter stand for the wider drug family.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dirt cheap costs next to nothing, a bargain bought for almost no money at all.

clue.text: Cleaning home or running errand, primarily?

definitions.text: Cleaning home or running errand, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.note: the initial letters of the five words

explanation.surface: Is housework or an errand really the main thing?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: its first letters spell the answer and the full clue describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleaning the house and running errands are typical examples of routine, tedious household tasks done out of duty.

clue.text: Live large with lustful revolutionary

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so these letters are turned back to front

blocks.note: lewd means lustful or lecherous
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A randy rebel lives it up in style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live large' reads as one phrase meaning to live extravagantly; it splits into the definition and the letter L.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell somewhere is to reside or have one's home there, a slightly formal synonym.

clue.text: We're told the writer observed ugly scene

indicators.note: being told something is hearing it spoken, so the words are taken by their sound

blocks.note: the writer refers to the setter as 'I'
to observe is to see; in non-rhotic speech the past tense rhymes with sore

explanation.surface: Rumour has it an author witnessed something hideous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I saw' spoken in a British accent matches the answer; 'the writer' is a common crossword way for the setter to say 'I'.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyesore is something unpleasant to look at, such as an ugly building spoiling a view.

clue.text: Earl reports landholdings

blocks.note: E is an abbreviation for Earl
to report is to state

explanation.surface: An aristocrat gives an account of his property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reports' looks like a noun, as in accounts, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is a large area of land in the country owned by one person or family, often with a big house.

clue.text: Boxers' ultimate sporting prize: they're worn like belts

indicators.note: ultimate means final, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the word, ignoring the apostrophe
the Ashes is the cricket trophy contested between England and Australia

explanation.surface: Boxing's greatest trophy is a championship belt worn round the waist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxers' ultimate sporting prize' reads as one phrase, a boxing title, but it splits into a last letter and the cricket trophy.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is a long strip of cloth worn round the waist or over one shoulder, much as a belt is.

clue.text: Everyman, very behind, deserted and alone

blocks.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as 'I'
so means very, as in 'so good'
lated is an old poetic word for belated, running behind time

explanation.surface: The setter, running late, feels abandoned and lonely.
explanation.walkthrough: Lated, as in Macbeth's 'lated traveller', is an archaic form of belated; the setter's own name stands for 'I'.
explanation.definitionFit: An isolated place is remote and empty, and an isolated person is cut off from others, lonely and solitary.
